In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a lot of progress in the field of learning motor skills for autonomous robots.
we have made a significant progress towards a general approach to learning motor skills in robots, but there is still much to do to achieve a truly general approach to this problem.

the current state of the art in machine learning is sufficient to solve a number of problems of robotics but that the field of robotics can still contribute to machine learning by providing a number of new problems, new data sets and new evaluation criteria.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the combination of the two approaches, i.e. a representation of motor skills based on the concept of a movement primitive, and a learning algorithm that can learn a movement primitive controller based on the concept, has been successfully demonstrated in several domains and has proven to scale to high-dimensional robotic systems.
the combination of these two aspects is a key ingredient for scaling learning algorithms to real world robotics tasks and that we have been able to show this in a number of domains.
the combination of a suitable control structure with appropriate learning methods can indeed enable robots to learn a variety of motor skills.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can successfully apply a general approach to learning motor skills which can be applied to a variety of tasks in a variety of domains.

the combination of a general task representation with a learning algorithm that can be used in this representation can indeed scale into high-dimensional domains and can be applied to a variety of different tasks, ranging from low-dimensional tasks like the control of a single joint to the control of a full humanoid robot.
the representation of motor skills is a key component for learning and that the choice of a learning method depends on the type of representation that is being employed.
